description:
I’m Michael Agyei Yeboah, a Full-Stack Software Engineer & AI Integration Specialist experienced in cloud architectures, web/mobile apps, and computer vision.

We’re building Aniwa ("Eye" in Twi) for Dancing with the SARs. It’s a real-time satellite platform tackling deforestation. Using cloud-penetrating NASA-ISRO (NISAR) & Sentinel-1 SAR data, Aniwa cuts through tropical clouds to deliver high-res canopy loss detection & early alerts. Looking for GIS, UI/UX, and devs to join us!
summary:
We built Aniwa, a live web platform that watches, predicts and alerts on deforestation in Ghana. Ghana has lost more than a fifth of its tree cover since 2001 to illegal logging, galamsey mining and farm clearing. Every dry season, bushfires set indiscriminately for hunting and land clearing, especially in the northern regions, also burn large areas of vegetation.

Aniwa combines NASA FIRMS active-fire detections (VIIRS and MODIS satellites), NASA POWER weather data, and Landsat-based forest-loss history and clearing alerts from Global Forest Watch. It tracks every fire the satellites detect across Ghana, scores deforestation risk across the forest belt, and maps the places most likely to be cleared next. Ordinary phones become forest listening devices: an on-device AI model recognises chainsaw sounds and pins each one on the map.

When the risk is real, Aniwa alerts rangers and communities instantly through Telegram, SMS and email. Anyone can also ask the Telegram bot for predictions, forest-loss figures or nearby fires.

Satellites alone often reveal damage weeks later. By adding on-the-ground sound and early warnings, Aniwa helps authorities act before the vegetation is gone, protecting wildlife, water and the people who depend on the land.
details:
LINKS

Live platform: https://aniwa-wine.vercel.app

Source code (GitHub): https://github.com/awuni1/Aniwa

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Aniwa is a live web platform that watches, predicts and alerts on deforestation in Ghana. It has three parts:

1. Satellite monitoring. Aniwa pulls near-real-time fire detections from NASA FIRMS (VIIRS on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, plus MODIS on Terra and Aqua), daily VIIRS satellite imagery from NASA GIBS, temperature data from NASA POWER, forest-loss history from Global Forest Watch (Hansen/UMD, built from Landsat) and recent clearing alerts (GLAD-L Landsat, GLAD-S2 Sentinel-2 and RADD Sentinel-1 radar). Everything is shown on an interactive map of Ghana, including the dry-season bushfires in the northern regions that are often set indiscriminately for hunting and land clearing.

2. Risk prediction. For every point in the forest belt, Aniwa calculates the chance of clearing using a transparent formula: P = sigmoid(-2.5 + F + T + A). F is past forest loss nearby (weighted by distance), T is tree cover from ESA WorldCover (forests with more trees have more to lose), and A is recent activity: chainsaw detections, fires, clearing alerts and hot, dry fire weather. Points are ranked severe, high or moderate, and each one shows the reasons behind its score.

3. Chainsaw listening. Any ordinary phone can become a forest listening device by opening the Aniwa /listen page. An AI sound model (Audio Spectrogram Transformer, trained on Google's AudioSet) runs on the phone itself and checks every 10 seconds for chainsaw sounds. A detection is pinned on the map with its location and score.

ALERTS

Every 30 minutes Aniwa checks for new fires in the forest belt and alerts rangers on Telegram. When two phones (or one phone twice) detect a chainsaw within 2 km and 10 minutes, rangers get a Telegram message and an SMS with a map link. Anyone can also message the Aniwa Telegram bot: /predict for the top risk areas, /forest for forest-loss figures, /fires for recent fires and /status for system health.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Satellites usually reveal clearing days or weeks after it happens. Aniwa adds on-the-ground sound and early warnings, so rangers and forestry authorities can respond while logging is still in progress and focus patrols on the areas most likely to be cleared next. Our goal is to help the Forestry Commission, community forest groups and conservation NGOs protect Ghana's remaining forests, wildlife (including endangered species such as the Roloway monkey and forest elephant), water sources and the communities who depend on them, at almost no cost.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS

- Framework: Next.js 16 and React 19, styled with Tailwind CSS 4

- Maps and 3D: MapLibre GL, Esri satellite imagery, NASA GIBS imagery, Three.js

- On-device AI: Transformers.js running the Audio Spectrogram Transformer in the phone's browser

- Data: NASA FIRMS, NASA GIBS, NASA POWER, Global Forest Watch, ESA WorldCover, Sentinel-2 via Microsoft Planetary Computer, GBIF species records, Meteomatics weather, FAOSTAT, OpenStreetMap, geoBoundaries

- AI assistant: Google Gemini 2.5 Flash

- Alerts: Telegram Bot API, Africa's Talking SMS, Brevo email

- Database and hosting: PostgreSQL on Supabase, deployed on Vercel, with cron-job.org for scheduled checks

- Hardware: no special hardware. Any smartphone, even an old one, works as a sensor.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Most forest-monitoring tools only look down from space. Aniwa also listens from the ground, turning donated or old phones into a low-cost acoustic sensor network, and combines both views in one risk score. The AI runs entirely on the phone, so it works without uploading audio. Alerts arrive through Telegram and SMS, channels rangers already use, instead of a dashboard they would have to keep checking.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Cost: free satellite data and ordinary phones instead of expensive acoustic hardware.

- Poor connectivity: detections are saved on the phone and sent when signal returns, and SMS reaches rangers without mobile data.

- Privacy: audio never leaves the phone. Only the time, location and score are sent.

- False alarms: chainsaw alerts need two nearby detections, and fire alerts ignore low-confidence detections and never repeat the same fire.

- Trust: the prediction formula is simple and explainable, and every risk area lists the reasons for its score.

- Local context: Ghana's forest belt, galamsey mining, dry-season bushfires and Harmattan fire weather.
